articles.title: Ofsted Reports Published for Laroche Day Care Nursery and Little Miracles Daycare
articles.excerpt: Ofsted has released inspection reports for Laroche Day Care Nursery and Little Miracles Daycare, detailing their findings and ratings. The reports were published on September 25 and 24, 2026, respectively.
articles.content_html:
Ofsted has published new inspection reports for two childcare providers in Rochdale: Laroche Day Care Nursery and Little Miracles Daycare. The report for Laroche Day Care Nursery was released on September 25, 2026, while the report for Little Miracles Daycare was published a day earlier, on September 24, 2026.

The inspection reports detail the findings from the assessments conducted at both nurseries, including any ratings awarded. Settings registered on the Early Years Register are typically inspected at least once within a four-year period, with newly registered settings inspected within 18 months of their registration. Ofsted prioritises inspections if there are concerns about a provider's performance, ensuring that quality standards are maintained in early years education.

Parents and guardians can access the full reports on the Ofsted website, where they can also find information about other childcare providers in Rochdale. This transparency is part of Ofsted's commitment to ensuring quality in early years education and care, allowing families to make informed choices regarding childcare services.

For those interested in receiving updates, Ofsted offers a subscription service that notifies users when new reports are published for specific providers. Further details can be found on the Ofsted contact page, which also provides information on how to reach out with any questions regarding the inspection process.

articles.title: Rochdale Opens Fourth Children's Home 'Diamond' to Support Local Young People
articles.excerpt: Rochdale Borough Council has opened its fourth children's home, named 'Diamond', as part of a £3.4 million investment to provide local care for children with complex needs.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Borough Council has officially opened its fourth children's home, named 'Diamond', as part of a £3.4 million investment aimed at expanding residential care provision for children in the area. This new home will accommodate three children with complex needs and disabilities who come into care, providing them with a supportive and homely environment.

The Diamond home features a dedicated sensory room, designed to cater to the specific needs of its residents. This opening marks the completion of a quartet of new homes, which also includes 'Emerald', 'Sapphire', and 'Ruby'. The names were chosen following suggestions from children in care, reflecting their input in the development process.

Councillor Rachel Massey, cabinet member for children's services and education, expressed her delight at the opening, stating that the new home will significantly improve the lives of children and young people in need of support. The initiative aims to ensure that more children can remain within their local community rather than being placed in care far from home, which has been a growing concern for local councils across the country.

With the addition of Diamond, the total number of placements available across the four homes now stands at 12. This expansion comes at a crucial time, as local authorities continue to face challenges in finding suitable placements for children in care. The council's investment is intended to provide a warm and comforting environment for these vulnerable young people, helping them to thrive in a familiar setting.

articles.title: Rochdale Libraries Partner with Charity to Provide Free School Uniforms
articles.excerpt: Libraries across Rochdale are collaborating with the charity Uniform For All to distribute free pre-loved school uniforms and shoes to families in need, helping to alleviate the financial burden of school costs.
articles.content_html:
Libraries across Rochdale are collaborating with the local charity Uniform For All to provide families with access to thousands of free pre-loved school uniforms and shoes. This initiative aims to support households struggling with the rising costs of school uniforms, which can often be a financial burden for many families.

Every day, high-quality pre-loved items such as polo shirts, skirts, trousers, branded school blazers, coats, and pumps are distributed through the charity. However, some families face challenges in travelling long distances to collect these items. To address this issue, Rochdale's library service is facilitating the collection of these uniforms, allowing families to pick them up at their nearest library, thereby reducing travel costs.

In addition to uniform collection, library staff will be available to provide families with information regarding the cost of living and related support services. Libraries also offer free Wi-Fi, computer access, and other benefits associated with library membership, creating a supportive environment for families in need.

Councillor Sue Smith, cabinet member for communities and co-operation, expressed her support for the initiative, highlighting its importance in helping families access essential school items without the added financial strain. This partnership between libraries and Uniform For All is expected to make a significant difference in the community, particularly as the new school year approaches.

Witnesses reported that families, including children, were present during the altercation, raising concerns about the safety of patrons at the family-friendly venue. One victim expressed feeling vulnerable and shocked by the incident, particularly given that it occurred in a workplace setting.

Hulme has a history of violence, with 19 previous offences, including an assault conviction from 2009. During the court proceedings, she claimed to have a 'vague' recollection of the events. The case highlights ongoing concerns regarding public safety in community spaces, particularly where families gather.

articles.title: Are there really fairies in Healey Dell?
articles.excerpt: The rocky 'Fairies’ Chapel' in Healey Dell is part geology and industrial history — and part long‑running local folklore; here’s what we can verify and what belongs to story.
articles.summary: The rocky 'Fairies’ Chapel' in Healey Dell is part geology and industrial history — and part long‑running local folklore; here’s what we can verify and what belongs to story.
articles.body:
If you’ve stood beneath the arches of Healey Dell viaduct and peered into the Thrutch — a narrow, water‑scoured cleft in the Spodden — you’ll understand why people once spoke of a tiny chapel for otherworldly folk. The spot called the Fairies’ Chapel is a named feature inside Healey Dell Nature Reserve, which is run as a visitor site with a heritage centre and tea rooms on Dell Road. The reserve’s public information and the borough’s park listings make clear that Healey Dell is first and foremost a place of wildlife, waterfalls and industrial archaeology. ([rochdale.gov.uk](https://www.rochdale.gov.uk/directory-record/737/healey-dell-nature-reserve-and-tea-rooms-rochdale))

The core, verifiable landscape fact is straightforward: the River Spodden has cut into the local sandstone to create caverns, ledges and a pulpit‑like alcove in the gorge that people have long compared to a small chapel. Victorian and later visitors described seats and a pulpit formed by eroded rock; an 1838 flood is recorded locally as having altered the feature. Those geological and historical descriptions are what explain the place‑name — not any documentary evidence of supernatural beings. Local heritage material presents the “chapel” as a reading of natural rock formations rather than as a constructed building. ([healeydelltearooms.co.uk](https://www.healeydelltearooms.co.uk/history/))

The charming stories that give Healey Dell its fairy reputation come from the county’s older folklore tradition, preserved in 19th‑century collections. John Roby’s Traditions of Lancashire contains the best‑known account of the Fairies’ Chapel: a romantic narrative of millers, an enchanted cleft called the Thrutch, a Fairy Queen and a small bearded figure (sometimes called the Healey Dwarf) who features in meetings at the chapel. Roby collected and retold local tales in a literary style; his book helped fix versions of the story in print, but it is a record of oral tradition and imaginative retelling rather than a primary archival report of events. ([gutenberg.org](https://www.gutenberg.org/files/25256/25256-h/25256-h.htm))

Later nineteenth‑ and twentieth‑century guidebooks and local leaflets repeated and embellished Roby’s tales, mixing fairies with witches, prophecy and other colourful motifs. Modern interpretation at the Healey Dell Heritage Centre treats these stories explicitly as folklore for visitors — there is a place for storytelling, performances and a children’s “Fairy Grotto,” but the centre’s materials separate those tales from the documented history of mills, bridges and the disused Rochdale–Bacup railway. If you want to hear the legends, the heritage centre is where they are told; if you want to see the historical record, the viaduct, mill remains and council descriptions are the source. ([healeydelltearooms.co.uk](https://www.healeydelltearooms.co.uk/attractions/))

The viaduct that frames much of the Dell’s scenery is itself a protected historic structure: Healey Dell Viaduct is a Grade II listed Victorian railway viaduct, recorded on the National Heritage List for England and described in detail by Historic England (listing first entered 30 November 1984). That listing documents the industrial past that shaped the valley — the mills, tramways and railway infrastructure — and anchors the Dell’s public significance in tangible, dated engineering heritage rather than in folklore. ([historicengland.org.uk](https://historicengland.org.uk/listing/the-list/list-entry/1317784))

So: are there really fairies in Healey Dell? As a matter of verifiable fact, there is no documentary evidence that supernatural beings have met in the Thrutch. The “Fairies’ Chapel” name and the stories attached to it are part of Lancashire’s long oral and printed folklore tradition, powerfully popularised in the nineteenth century and kept alive locally through guides, performances and family storytelling. Those tales are valuable — they tell us how people have looked at landscape and memory — but they belong to culture and imagination rather than to the official historical record. Visitors can enjoy both the rock‑cut chapel and the stories it inspired, remembering to keep the two kinds of truth — geological and folkloric — clearly apart.

articles.title: Rochdale Health Leaders Present Collaborative Care Model at European Conference
articles.excerpt: Health leaders from Rochdale showcased their integrated healthcare model at an international conference in Belgium, highlighting the importance of collaboration in improving patient care.
articles.content_html:
Health leaders from Rochdale, Greater Manchester, presented their collaborative working model at the International Conference on Integrated Care held in Antwerp, Belgium. The event attracted over 1,000 delegates, where they shared insights on improving health and social care services.

Dr Salman Shahid, Associate Medical Director of the Greater Manchester Integrated Care Board, led the presentation alongside a team from One Rochdale Health and Care. They focused on the 'Integration Continuum' and its role in achieving patient-centred care within an integrated healthcare framework.

During the conference, Dr Shahid emphasised the need for a multi-disciplinary approach to tackle health inequalities in Rochdale, which is one of ten areas in Greater Manchester facing significant challenges. He noted the importance of collaboration among hospitals, community services, GP practices, and voluntary organisations to enhance patient and public involvement in health services.

Dr Shahid, along with colleagues Dr Kirsty Marshall, Dr Shona McCallum, and Alison Kelly, highlighted their work on improving patient engagement in health and social care. They discussed how their integrated approach aims to create a seamless health and well-being model with shared responsibility for patient care.

The conference provided an opportunity for Rochdale's health leaders to learn from colleagues across Europe, aiming to refine their approaches and ultimately improve the health and well-being of residents in the region. Dr Shahid stated that the insights gained would help enhance their systems and create a better health and social care framework for local residents.

articles.title: Rochdale Town Hall Renovation Wins Europa Nostra Award
articles.excerpt: The renovation of Rochdale Town Hall has received the prestigious Europa Nostra award, recognising its excellence in heritage conservation following a £20 million restoration project.
articles.content_html:
The renovation of Rochdale Town Hall has been honoured with the Europa Nostra award, one of Europe’s most prestigious accolades for heritage conservation. This award comes as part of a series of recognitions for the Grade I-listed building, which reopened fully last year after a £20 million restoration project.

The Europa Nostra award is particularly significant, as it was awarded to only three projects out of 261 applications across Europe. This latest accolade complements previous honours for the town hall, including the Civic Trust Awards, where it received the Michael Middleton Special Award for Excellence in Conservation and a Civic Trust Conservation Award.

In June 2026, the project also garnered four awards at the Royal Institute of British Architects (RIBA) North West Awards, including the RIBA North West Award 2026 and the RIBA North West Project Architect of the Year 2026. Additionally, it was recognised as the Social Project of the Year at the Association for Project Management (APM) Awards 2025, highlighting its positive impact on the community and economy.

The ongoing recognition of Rochdale Town Hall's renovation underscores its importance not only as a historical landmark but also as a centre for community engagement and cultural heritage. The town hall continues to serve as a venue for various events and activities, contributing to the local community's vibrancy.

articles.title: Peacocks to Open New Store at Rochdale Riverside as Footfall Increases by 15.3%
articles.excerpt: British clothing retailer Peacocks has signed a long-term lease for a unit at Rochdale Riverside, contributing to a 15.3% rise in footfall at the shopping centre.
articles.content_html:
British clothing retailer Peacocks has secured a long-term lease for a 10,181 sq ft unit at Rochdale Riverside, which is now 92% occupied. The store is set to open at the beginning of October 2026, further enhancing the shopping and leisure offerings at the centre.

The announcement follows a significant 15.3% increase in footfall at Rochdale Riverside, with nearly 200,000 visitors recorded in July alone. This upward trend in visitor numbers has been consistent throughout 2026, indicating a growing interest in the retail destination since its opening in Spring 2020.

Rochdale Riverside, which spans 200,000 sq ft, features a mix of shopping, dining, and leisure options, anchored by a 50,000 sq ft Marks & Spencer store and a six-screen Real Cinema. Other national retailers at the centre include Next, H&M, Boots, and JD Sports. Ollie Holland, asset manager for Rochdale Riverside at RivingtonHark, expressed confidence in the centre's appeal, stating that the addition of Peacocks reflects strong demand for well-located retail space.

Councillor Danny Meredith, cabinet member for regeneration and housing at Rochdale Borough Council, welcomed the new store, noting that it would be a popular addition to the shopping centre. Peacocks, established in 1884 and now operating 345 stores across the UK, is known for its budget-friendly clothing options, which will complement the existing retail mix at Rochdale Riverside.

articles.title: Failsworth Tram Stop Lift Out of Service Due to Replacement Works
articles.excerpt: The lift at Failsworth Tram Stop is currently out of service, affecting access for passengers. Those needing step-free access should travel to Hollinwood.
articles.content_html:
The lift at Failsworth Tram Stop, which services the platform heading towards Rochdale, is currently out of service due to replacement works. This situation has been in effect since 6:48am on Thursday, 24 September 2026, and will continue until further notice.

As a result of the lift being out of service, there is no step-free access available at this stop. Passengers requiring step-free access are advised to make their way to Hollinwood Tram Stop to connect to services.

Customers needing assistance or additional journey planning support are encouraged to contact the Metrolink customer service centre at 0161 244 1000. The lines are open from 7am to 8pm on weekdays and from 8am to 8pm on weekends and Bank Holidays.

This disruption may affect local commuters and those travelling to and from Rochdale, so passengers should plan their journeys accordingly.
